title: Why You Should Care If Your Students Dislike You https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/01/02/why-you-should-care-if-your-students-dislike-you/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by overhearing a teacher use sarcasm and anger on two students who ran in a hallway, Linsin argues that likability is not a soft nicety but a functional necessity for effective classroom management. He explains that when students dislike a teacher, the teacher's only real influence becomes negative — lecturing, scolding, yelling, and sarcasm — which curbs behavior only momentarily and causes students to blame the teacher rather than take responsibility for consequences. Conversely, likability gives consequences symbolic weight, since being separated from a classroom students genuinely enjoy, led by a teacher they admire, becomes a meaningful and effective deterrent on its own. He describes the ideal as a 'yin and yang' balance between an influential, warm relationship with students and an unwavering commitment to the classroom management plan, arguing neither works well without the other.
points: Sarcasm and visible anger toward students, however well-intentioned, tend to build dislike and undermine authority.
When students dislike a teacher, only negative tools (yelling, scolding, sarcasm) remain effective, and only in the moment.
Likability makes consequences meaningful because being separated from an admired teacher and enjoyed classroom carries real weight.
The most effective teachers balance genuine warmth and likability with unwavering enforcement of a classroom management plan.
quotes: Besides being difficult for children to understand, sarcasm is cruel. It is meant to make the target of the remark feel inadequate and elevate the speaker to a position of superiority.

If you are disliked, the only influence you have with students is negative (i.e., lecturing, scolding, yelling, and sarcasm). And negativity only works to curb bad behavior in the moment. It does nothing to improve behavior over time.
Being disliked also weakens the power of your consequences to curb unwanted behavior. When you enforce a consequence, instead of taking responsibility, your students will most likely blame you.

Likeability gives meaning to consequences and underscores the feeling of separation students feel when held apart from the classroom they love being a part of, by the teacher they admire. This can be a very powerful consequence.

The most effective teachers are able to balance an influential relationship with students (i.e., being fun, likeable, creating exciting lessons) with an unwavering commitment to their classroom management plan. You can’t have one without the other.
